newsitem.title: USA: Dollar up on German endorsement, talk of budget deal.
newsitem.headline: Dollar up on German endorsement, talk of budget deal.

text.p: The dollar rose against most major currencies on Tuesday after an important group of German economists predicted it would rally in coming months and U.S. negotiators reportedly neared a deal on the federal budget.
The dollar also benefited from official Japanese comments suggesting major central banks would not enter the markets to stop the dollar's rise against the Japanese yen.

"This market does like to test the toleration level of the central banks (for the dollar) and we have yet to find that level," said Seth Garrett, a director of foreign exchange at Credit Suisse First Boston.
A group of six leading German economic research institutes predicted in their semiannual report that the dollar would trade at an average rate of 1.80 German marks in 1998.
That helped the dollar rally to 1.7160 marks late Tuesday, up from 1.6982 late Monday.

"I don't see a strong economy in Germany and the fundamental picture is much better (in the United States). I think within six months we could see the dollar at 1.80 marks," said James Powers, vice president of corporate foreign exchange at Westdeutsche Landesbank Girozentrale.

The dollar also rose to 126.32 Japanese yen from 125.34 late Monday and 1.4622 Swiss francs from 1.4418. The British pound fell to $1.6345 from $1.6355. The dollar fell to Canadian $1.3952 from C$1.3986.
Rumours swirled throughout the U.S. trading session that Congressional and White House negotiators were close to agreement on a plan to balance the federal budget by the year 2002.
Late in the day, a White House spokesman said President Bill Clinton would discuss the budget with Congressional Democrats on Wednesday.
U.S. stocks and bonds also rallied on the news, helping the dollar move to fresh highs.
"A budget deal would definitely be bullish in the short term," said Garrett.

The dollar got a boost in early Asian trading when Japan's Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told parliament not to expect aggressive support for the ailing yen at an official meeting of the Group of Seven industrial nations this weekend in Washington.

Mitsuzuka said the meeting would probably produce a statement similar to one released at the February G7 meeting in Berlin, which simply said the group would deal with excessive currency movements as appropriate.
"The market took that as a sign the United States and Germany don't care about the strong dollar as much as Japan does," said Powers.
Yet investors refrained from making aggressive bets on the dollar ahead of the meeting as a precaution against a surprise statement or market intervention to weaken the dollar.
"Nobody wants to take the dollar too high before the G7 meets," said Mike Malpede, senior foreign exchange analyst at Refco Group Ltd.
Comments from a Swiss official helped accelerate the dollar's rise against European currencies, dealers said.
Swiss National Bank Vice Chairman Jean-Pierre Roth said he saw no reason to expect Swiss interest rates to move in either direction in the near term.
Traders interpreted that as a sign the SNB sees the Swiss economy as too weak to tolerate higher interest rates, which would tend to boost the Swiss franc.
"That's partly why the dollar was so strong," Malpede said.
